A Conjecture on Circular Permutations over Finite FieldsThanks: The second author was supported by the Tian Yuan Mathematical Foundation (Grant No. 12526613).

Xin-Qi Luo Address: School of Sciences, Changzhou Institute of Technology, Changzhou 213032, China Email address: luoxq@czust.edu.cn and Yue-Feng She Address: Department of Applied Mathematics, Nanjing Forestry University, Nanjing 210037, China Email address: she.math@njfu.edu.cn
Abstract.

Let 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} be a finite field with q>7q>7. Zhi-Wei Sun conjectured that for every a0∈𝔽qa_{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, there is a circular permutation (a1,…,aq−1)(a_{1},\dots,a_{q-1}) of non-zero elements of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} such that a0+ai​ai+1a_{0}+a_{i}a_{i+1} is primitive for 1≤i≤q−11\leq i\leq q-1, where aq=a1a_{q}=a_{1}. In this paper, we confirm this conjecture for q>18 888 871q>18\,888\,871. For a0=0a_{0}=0, the conclusion holds for all q>4q>4. For a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0, we apply the Chvátal–Erdős theorem to obtain a Hamilton cycle.

Key words and phrases: 
Hamiltonicity, finite field, primitive element
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary 05C45; Secondary 11A07

1. Introduction

Let 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} be a finite field of order q=pfq=p^{f}, with pp prime and ff a positive integer. We denote the multiplicative group of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} by 𝔽q∗.\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. The generators of 𝔽q∗\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} are called primitive elements. Permutations satisfying arithmetic restrictions and primitive elements in finite fields lead to many interesting problems. In 1982, Filz [4] conjectured that for every even nn, there is a permutation τ\tau of {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\} such that

τ⁡(1)+τ⁡(2),τ⁡(2)+τ⁡(3),…,τ⁡(n)+τ⁡(1)\tau(1)+\tau(2),\ \tau(2)+\tau(3),\ \dots,\ \tau(n)+\tau(1)

are all prime. This conjecture appears in Guy’s book [5]. For recent progress on this problem, one may refer to [2, 6, 7].

Primitive elements and permutations lead to several questions. In 2013, Sun [9] proposed a series of conjectures on permutations of finite fields. For example, Sun and Hou [9, Conjecture 3.5(i)] conjectured that there is a circular permutation of the elements of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} for q>7q>7 such that every adjacent sum is primitive. This conjecture has recently been confirmed by the second author for q>18 888 871q>18\,888\,871 [7].

In this paper, we study another conjecture of Sun [9, Conjecture 3.8].

Conjecture 1.1.

Let 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} be a finite field with q>7q>7. For any given element a0∈𝔽qa_{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, there exists a circular permutation (a1,…,aq−1)(a_{1},\dots,a_{q-1}) of all elements of 𝔽q∗\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} such that

a0+a1​a2,a0+a2​a3,…,a0+aq−2​aq−1,a0+aq−1​a1a_{0}+a_{1}a_{2},\quad a_{0}+a_{2}a_{3},\quad\dots,\quad a_{0}+a_{q-2}a_{q-1},\quad a_{0}+a_{q-1}a_{1}

are primitive elements of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}.

For a graph GG, its vertex set and edge set are denoted by V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G), respectively. Given a0∈𝔽qa_{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, we define a graph Gq,a0G_{q,a_{0}} with V⁡(Gq,a0)=𝔽q∗V(G_{q,a_{0}})=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} by

x​y∈E⁡(Gq,a0)⟺x≠y​ and ​a0+x​y​ is primitive.xy\in E(G_{q,a_{0}})\Longleftrightarrow x\neq y\text{ and }a_{0}+xy\text{ is primitive.}

The desired circular permutation is exactly a Hamilton cycle in Gq,a0G_{q,a_{0}}.

Theorem 1.2.

For any prime power q>18 888 871q>18\,888\,871 and any a0∈𝔽qa_{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}, Gq,a0G_{q,a_{0}} is Hamiltonian. When a0=0a_{0}=0, the conclusion holds for q>4q>4.

2. Preliminaries

For a positive integer nn, let ω⁡(n)\omega(n), φ⁡(n)\varphi(n) and μ⁡(n)\mu(n) denote the number of distinct prime divisors of nn, Euler’s totient function and the Möbius function, respectively. Define

W⁡(n)=2ω⁡(n)W(n)=2^{\omega(n)}

to be the number of squarefree divisors of nn. We let 𝔽q∗^\widehat{\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}} denote the group of multiplicative characters of 𝔽q∗\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. For any χ∈𝔽q∗^\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}}, we extend χ\chi to 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} by χ⁡(0)=0\chi(0)=0. The characteristic function of primitive elements in 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} is given by

(1) 𝟏prim​(x)=φ⁡(q−1)q−1​∑d|q−1μ⁡(d)φ⁡(d)​∑χ∈𝔽^q∗ord⁡(χ)=dχ⁡(x).\mathbf{1}_{\text{prim}}(x)=\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}\sum_{d\mid q-1}\frac{\mu(d)}{\varphi(d)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{*}\\ \operatorname{ord}(\chi)=d\end{subarray}}\chi(x).

For any graph GG, we write α⁡(G)\alpha(G) for its independence number, δ⁡(G)\delta(G) for its minimum degree, and κ⁡(G)\kappa(G) for its vertex connectivity. We will use the following theorem given by Chvátal and Erdős [1].

Theorem 2.1.

Let GG be a finite simple graph with at least three vertices. If κ⁡(G)≥α⁡(G)\kappa(G)\geq\alpha(G), then GG is Hamiltonian.

For X,Y⊆𝔽q∗X,Y\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}, define

E⁡(X,Y)=|{(x,y)∈X×Y:a0+x​y​ is primitive}|.E(X,Y)=|\{(x,y)\in X\times Y:a_{0}+xy\text{ is primitive}\}|.
Lemma 2.2.

For any subsets X,Y⊆𝔽q∗X,Y\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}, and any non-zero a0∈𝔽q∗a_{0}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}:

|E⁡(X,Y)−φ⁡(q−1)q−1​|X|​|Y||≤φ⁡(q−1)q−1​W​(q−1)​q​|X|​|Y|.\displaystyle\left|E(X,Y)-\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}|X||Y|\right|\leq\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}W(q-1)\sqrt{q|X||Y|}.
Proof.

By definition of E⁡(X,Y)E(X,Y) and (1),

E⁡(X,Y)=φ⁡(q−1)q−1​∑d|q−1μ⁡(d)φ⁡(d)​∑χ∈𝔽^q∗ord⁡(χ)=d∑x∈X∑y∈Yχ⁡(a0+x​y).E(X,Y)=\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}\sum_{d\mid q-1}\frac{\mu(d)}{\varphi(d)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\chi\in\widehat{\mathbb{F}}_{q}^{*}\\ \operatorname{ord}(\chi)=d\end{subarray}}\sum_{x\in X}\sum_{y\in Y}\chi(a_{0}+xy).

The principal multiplicative character term contributes

φ⁡(q−1)q−1​|X|​|Y|−φ⁡(q−1)q−1​T0,\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}|X||Y|-\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}T_{0},

where T0T_{0} is the number of solutions to a0+x​y=0a_{0}+xy=0 in X×YX\times Y. Since a0​x​y≠0a_{0}xy\neq 0, we have T0≤min⁡(|X|,|Y|)≤|X|​|Y|T_{0}\leq\min(|X|,|Y|)\leq\sqrt{|X||Y|}.

For any non-principal multiplicative character χ\chi, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives

|∑x∈X∑y∈Yχ⁡(a0+x​y)|2≤|X|∑x∈X|∑y∈Yχ⁡(a0+x​y)|2≤|X|​∑y1,y2∈Y∑x∈𝔽qχ⁡(a0+x​y1)​χ¯​(a0+x​y2).\left|\sum_{x\in X}\sum_{y\in Y}\chi(a_{0}+xy)\right|^{2}\leq|X|\sum_{x\in X}\left|\sum_{y\in Y}\chi(a_{0}+xy)\right|^{2}\leq|X|\sum_{y_{1},y_{2}\in Y}\sum_{x\in\mathbb{F}_{q}}\chi(a_{0}+xy_{1})\overline{\chi}(a_{0}+xy_{2}).

For y1=y2y_{1}=y_{2}, the inner sum is q−1q-1. For y1≠y2y_{1}\neq y_{2}, the inner sum is

∑x∈𝔽qx≠−a0​y2−1χ⁡(x​y1+a0x​y2+a0)=∑x∈𝔽qx≠−a0​y2−1χ⁡(y1y2+a0​(y2−y1)y2​(x​y2+a0))=−χ⁡(y1y2).\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\\ x\neq-a_{0}y_{2}^{-1}\end{subarray}}\chi\left(\frac{xy_{1}+a_{0}}{xy_{2}+a_{0}}\right)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\\ x\neq-a_{0}y_{2}^{-1}\end{subarray}}\chi\left(\frac{y_{1}}{y_{2}}+\frac{a_{0}(y_{2}-y_{1})}{y_{2}(xy_{2}+a_{0})}\right)=-\chi\left(\frac{y_{1}}{y_{2}}\right).

Therefore

|∑x∈X∑y∈Yχ⁡(a0+x​y)|2≤\displaystyle\left|\sum_{x\in X}\sum_{y\in Y}\chi(a_{0}+xy)\right|^{2}\leq |X|​((q−1)​|Y|−∑y1≠y2∈Yχ⁡(y1)​χ¯​(y2))\displaystyle|X|\left((q-1)|Y|-\sum_{y_{1}\neq y_{2}\in Y}\chi(y_{1})\overline{\chi}(y_{2})\right)
=\displaystyle= |X|​(q​|Y|−|∑y∈Yχ⁡(y)|2)\displaystyle|X|\left(q|Y|-\left|\sum_{y\in Y}\chi(y)\right|^{2}\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq q​|X|​|Y|.\displaystyle q|X||Y|.

Since there are exactly φ⁡(d)\varphi(d) multiplicative characters of order dd and W⁡(q−1)W(q-1) squarefree divisors of q−1q-1, combining the above, we obtain

|E⁡(X,Y)−φ⁡(q−1)q−1​|X|​|Y||≤\displaystyle\left|E(X,Y)-\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}|X||Y|\right|\leq φ⁡(q−1)q−1​|X|​|Y|+φ⁡(q−1)q−1​(W⁡(q−1)−1)​q​|X|​|Y|\displaystyle\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}\sqrt{|X||Y|}+\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}(W(q-1)-1)\sqrt{q|X||Y|}
≤\displaystyle\leq φ⁡(q−1)q−1​W​(q−1)​q​|X|​|Y|.\displaystyle\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}W(q-1)\sqrt{q|X||Y|}.

∎

3. The case of a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0

Throughout this section, we assume a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0. For simplicity, we write G=Gq,a0G=G_{q,a_{0}}.

Lemma 3.1.

The independence number of GG satisfies

α⁡(G)≤2​W​(q−1)​q+1.\alpha(G)\leq 2W(q-1)\sqrt{q}+1.
Proof.

Let I⊆𝔽q∗I\subseteq\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} be an independent set of maximum size s=α⁡(G)s=\alpha(G). We partition II into two disjoint subsets XX and YY with

|X|=⌊s2⌋and|Y|=⌈s2⌉.|X|=\left\lfloor\frac{s}{2}\right\rfloor\quad\text{and}\quad|Y|=\left\lceil\frac{s}{2}\right\rceil.

Since II is independent, there are no edges between XX and YY, so E⁡(X,Y)=0E(X,Y)=0. Applying Lemma 2.2, we have

φ⁡(q−1)q−1​|X|​|Y|≤φ⁡(q−1)q−1​W​(q−1)​q​|X|​|Y|.\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}|X||Y|\leq\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}W(q-1)\sqrt{q|X||Y|}.

Hence

⌊s2⌋​⌈s2⌉≤W⁡(q−1)​q.\sqrt{\left\lfloor\frac{s}{2}\right\rfloor\left\lceil\frac{s}{2}\right\rceil}\leq W(q-1)\sqrt{q}.

If ss is even, we have

s≤2​W​(q−1)​q.s\leq 2W(q-1)\sqrt{q}.

If ss is odd, we have

s≤s2−1+1≤2​W​(q−1)​q+1s\leq\sqrt{s^{2}-1}+1\leq 2W(q-1)\sqrt{q}+1

This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma 3.2.

The vertex connectivity of GG satisfies

κ⁡(G)≥φ⁡(q−1)−W⁡(q−1)​q−1.\kappa(G)\geq\varphi(q-1)-W(q-1)\sqrt{q}-1.
Proof.

Let S⊆V⁡(G)=𝔽q∗S\subseteq V(G)=\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} be a minimum vertex cut of GG, that is, |S|=κ⁡(G)|S|=\kappa(G). Given any vertex v∈𝔽q∗v\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}, a0+v​ya_{0}+vy ranges over 𝔽q∖{a0}\mathbb{F}_{q}\setminus\{a_{0}\} as yy ranges over 𝔽q∗\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*}. Since a0a_{0} and a0+v2a_{0}+v^{2} may be primitive, we have

(2) δ⁡(G)≥φ⁡(q−1)−2.\delta(G)\geq\varphi(q-1)-2.

Let AA be a smallest connected component of G−SG-S, and let B=V⁡(G)∖(A∪S)B=V(G)\setminus(A\cup S). For any a∈Aa\in A, as there are no edges between AA and BB, all its neighbors in GG lie in A∪SA\cup S with at most |A|−1|A|-1 neighbors inside AA. Therefore, aa must have at least deg⁡(a)−(|A|−1)\deg(a)-(|A|-1) neighbors in SS where deg⁡(a)\deg(a) is the degree of aa. Thus

(3) κ⁡(G)≥δ⁡(G)−(|A|−1)=δ⁡(G)−|A|+1.\kappa(G)\geq\delta(G)-(|A|-1)=\delta(G)-|A|+1.

In addition, applying Lemma 2.2 to X=AX=A and Y=BY=B with E⁡(A,B)=0E(A,B)=0, we obtain that

φ⁡(q−1)q−1​|A|​|B|≤φ⁡(q−1)q−1​W​(q−1)​q​|A|​|B|.\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}|A||B|\leq\frac{\varphi(q-1)}{q-1}W(q-1)\sqrt{q|A||B|}.

Hence

|A|≤|A|​|B|≤W⁡(q−1)​q.|A|\leq\sqrt{|A||B|}\leq W(q-1)\sqrt{q}.

This, together with equations (2) and (3), gives the desired lower bound for κ⁡(G)\kappa(G). ∎

Inspired by the approach of Cohen, Oliveira e Silva, and Trudgian [3], we divide our proof into three cases.

Proof of Theorem 1.2 when a0≠0a_{0}\neq 0.

By Theorem 2.1, Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2, it suffices to show that

(4) φ⁡(q−1)≥3​W​(q−1)​q+2\varphi(q-1)\geq 3W(q-1)\sqrt{q}+2

for any prime power q>18 888 871q>18\,888\,871. Put n=q−1n=q-1 and let r=ω⁡(n)r=\omega(n). Write

n=∏j=1rℓjaj,n=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\ell_{j}^{a_{j}},

where ℓ1<⋯<ℓr\ell_{1}<\dots<\ell_{r} are primes and aj≥1a_{j}\geq 1. We define Pr=p1​p2​…​prP_{r}=p_{1}p_{2}\ldots p_{r}, where pjp_{j} denotes the jj-th prime. Since

φ⁡(n)n=∏j=1r(1−1ℓj),\frac{\varphi(n)}{n}=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\left(1-\frac{1}{\ell_{j}}\right),

it increases as any prime divisor ℓj\ell_{j} increases. Hence,

φ⁡(n)n≥αr:=φ⁡(Pr)Pr.\frac{\varphi(n)}{n}\geq\alpha_{r}:=\frac{\varphi(P_{r})}{P_{r}}.

Since

φ⁡(n)n=∏j=1rℓj(aj−1)/2⋅ℓj−1ℓj,\frac{\varphi(n)}{\sqrt{n}}=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\ell_{j}^{(a_{j}-1)/2}\cdot\dfrac{\ell_{j}-1}{\sqrt{\ell_{j}}},

by the monotonicity of (x−1)/x(x-1)/\sqrt{x}, we have

φ⁡(n)n≥βr:=φ⁡(Pr)Pr.\frac{\varphi(n)}{\sqrt{n}}\geq\beta_{r}:=\frac{\varphi(P_{r})}{\sqrt{P_{r}}}.

Case 1: r≥9r\geq 9. Note that for every k≥10k\geq 10,

pk−1pk>2.\frac{p_{k}-1}{\sqrt{p_{k}}}>2.

Thus we obtain

βr2r=β92r​∏k=10rpk−1pk≥β9​ 2−9>4.772.\frac{\beta_{r}}{2^{r}}=\frac{\beta_{9}}{2^{r}}\prod_{k=10}^{r}\frac{p_{k}-1}{\sqrt{p_{k}}}\geq\beta_{9}\,2^{-9}>4.772.

Since n≥18 888 871n\geq 18\,888\,871,

3​1+1n+22r​n<3.001.\displaystyle 3\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{n}}+\frac{2}{2^{r}\sqrt{n}}<3.001.

Thus

φ⁡(n)n≥βr>3⋅2r​1+1n+2n\frac{\varphi(n)}{\sqrt{n}}\geq\beta_{r}>3\cdot 2^{r}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{n}}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{n}}

and (4) follows.

Case 2: r=8r=8. Suppose that nn is squarefree. If ℓ8≥43\ell_{8}\geq 43, then

n≥2⋅3⋅5⋅7⋅11⋅13⋅17⋅43=21 951 930n\geq 2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 43=21\,951\,930

and

φ⁡(n)n≥α8​n≥16588809699690​21 951 930>801.29.\frac{\varphi(n)}{\sqrt{n}}\geq\alpha_{8}\sqrt{n}\geq\frac{1658880}{9699690}\sqrt{21\,951\,930}>801.29.

For fixed ℓ8<43\ell_{8}<43, we check all possible choices of ℓ1,…,ℓ7\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{7} with

n=ℓ1⋯ℓ8>18 888 870.n=\ell_{1}\cdots\ell_{8}>18\,888\,870.

and n+1n+1 a prime power. Among all squarefree n>18 888 870n>18\,888\,870, the minimum of φ⁡(n)/n\varphi(n)/\sqrt{n} is at

(ℓ1,…,ℓ8)=(2,3,5,7,11,13,23,29),(\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{8})=(2,3,5,7,11,13,23,29),

for which n=20 030 010,n=20\,030\,010, and

φ⁡(n)n>792.70.\frac{\varphi(n)}{\sqrt{n}}>792.70.

Suppose nn is not squarefree. The least non-squarefree n>18 888 870n>18\,888\,870 with n+1n+1 a prime power is

n=22⋅3⋅5⋅7⋅11⋅13⋅17⋅31=31 651 620.n=2^{2}\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 7\cdot 11\cdot 13\cdot 17\cdot 31=31\,651\,620.

Therefore

φ⁡(n)n≥α8​n>962.01.\frac{\varphi(n)}{\sqrt{n}}\geq\alpha_{8}\sqrt{n}>962.01.

In summary, we have

φ⁡(n)n>792.70.\frac{\varphi(n)}{\sqrt{n}}>792.70.

Moreover,

3⋅28​1+1n+2n<768.013\cdot 2^{8}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{n}}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{n}}<768.01

for n>18 888 870n>18\,888\,870. Thus (4) holds.

Case 3: 1≤r≤71\leq r\leq 7. Since

αr≥α7=307217017,\alpha_{r}\geq\alpha_{7}=\frac{3072}{17017},

and n>18 888 870n>18\,888\,870, we have

φ⁡(n)n≥α7​n>784.56>384.01>3⋅2r​1+1n+2n.\frac{\varphi(n)}{\sqrt{n}}\geq\alpha_{7}\sqrt{n}>784.56>384.01>3\cdot 2^{r}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{n}}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{n}}.

So (4) holds.

Combining Cases 1, 2 and 3, GG is Hamiltonian when q>18 888 871q>18\,888\,871. ∎

4. The case of a0=0a_{0}=0

Our construction for odd prime powers qq is inspired by Sinha, Garg and Singh [8].

Proof of Theorem 1.2 when a0=0a_{0}=0.

Let gg be a primitive element of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} and let n=q−1n=q-1. Any ai∈𝔽q∗a_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{*} can be represented uniquely by its exponent with respect to gg, that is,

ai=gxifor some unique ​xi∈{0,1,…,n−1}.a_{i}=g^{x_{i}}\quad\text{for some unique }x_{i}\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}.

The adjacent product ai​ai+1=gxi+xi+1a_{i}a_{i+1}=g^{x_{i}+x_{i+1}} is a primitive element of 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} if and only if

gcd⁡(xi+xi+1,n)=1.\gcd(x_{i}+x_{i+1},\,n)=1.

We construct the Hamilton cycle by considering the parity of nn separately.

If nn is even, consider the sequence

(x1,x2,…,xn,x1)=(0,n−1, 2,n−3, 4,n−5,…,n−2, 1, 0).(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n},x_{1})=(0,\,n-1,\,2,\,n-3,\,4,\,n-5,\,\dots,\,n-2,\,1,\,0).

It yields a Hamilton cycle in Gq,0G_{q,0}.

If nn is odd, write n=2​h+1n=2h+1, where h≥2h\geq 2. When h=2h=2, we have q=6q=6, which is not a prime power. For h=3h=3, we have

(x1,x2,…,x7,x1)=(6,0,5,1,3,2,4,6).(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{7},x_{1})=(6,0,5,1,3,2,4,6).

and every adjacent sum is coprime to 77. For h≥4,h\geq 4, consider the sequence

(x1,x2,…,xn,x1)=(n−1,0,n−2,1,h,h−1,h+1,h−2,h+2,…,2,n−3,n−1).(x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n},x_{1})=(n-1,0,n-2,1,h,h-1,h+1,h-2,h+2,\ldots,2,n-3,n-1).

In this sequence, every adjacent sum is congruent to n−1n-1, n−2n-2, n−4n-4 or h+1h+1 modulo nn. Since

gcd⁡(n−1,n)=gcd⁡(n−2,n)=gcd⁡(n−4,n)=gcd⁡(h+1,n)=1,\gcd(n-1,n)=\gcd(n-2,n)=\gcd(n-4,n)=\gcd(h+1,n)=1,

this leads to a Hamilton cycle in Gq,0G_{q,0}. This completes the proof. ∎
